narrative:
The model estimated a 54.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, it judged failure slightly more likely than passing, so your application was denied. This is a risk estimate, not a certainty.

The largest driver was your LSAT score, which at 25 was well below the 37.18 average among accepted students and pushed the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most important factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.30 it was slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, so it pushed toward passing and partly offset the LSAT result. The third factor was your year-three class-rank decile, where 4.00 was below the accepted average of 5.79; however, its modeled influence was the smallest of the three and leaned toward passing.

To improve your position, ask the admissions office for specific feedback and whether an appeal or additional review is available. Consider retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, since that was the dominant negative factor. You can also submit an explanatory statement for any contextual issues and evidence of academic improvement, and consider reapplying to programs with holistic or conditional admission. Strengthening your LSAT result and presenting a clearer bar-readiness plan would most directly address the reason for denial.
